content_voiceover: This slide presents the pivotal trial data for etranacogene dezaparvovec, the AAV5-based gene therapy for hemophilia B that carries the hyperfunctional Padua variant of factor IX. On the left, the box plots track factor IX activity from baseline through 18 months, showing a steady climb from essentially undetectable levels to a durable plateau in the mean range of roughly 35 to 40 percent of normal activity, which is enough to reclassify most patients from severe to mild hemophilia B. On the right, the annualized bleeding rate comparison is the headline result, patients averaged 4.19 annualized bleeds during the lead-in observation period, which dropped to 1.51 after gene therapy, and this represents a bleeding rate ratio of 0.36, meaning roughly a 64% relative reduction, with a P value under 0.001. Importantly, this study was designed as a noninferiority trial against prophylactic factor IX replacement, with a prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.8, and the observed ratio of 0.36 easily fell within that margin, actually demonstrating superiority over standard factor IX prophylaxis rather than just noninferiority.
keypoints: Etranacogene dezaparvovec raised factor IX activity to a durable mean around 35 to 40 percent of normal
Annualized bleeding rate fell from 4.19 in lead-in to 1.51 post-treatment, a rate ratio of 0.36
Trial met its noninferiority margin of 1.8 and showed superiority over prophylactic factor IX replacement
Uses the Padua variant of factor IX, which has 8 to 12 times normal specific activity
keypoint_voiceover: High yield point, this Padua-variant gene therapy for hemophilia B didn't just meet noninferiority against standard factor IX prophylaxis, it demonstrated superiority, with a bleeding rate ratio of 0.36 and a noninferiority margin of 1.8.
